content: Health promotion has been defined by the 2005 Bangkok Charter for Health Promotion in a Globalized World as the process of enabling people to increase control over their health and its determinants, and thereby improve their health. Methods of health promotion include health education and social marketing. The earliest and most well-known definition of health promotion, as stated by the American Journal of Health Promotion since at least 1986, is the science and art of helping people change their lifestyle to move toward a state of optimal health. This definition was derived from the 1974 Lalonde Report from the Government of Canada, which outlined a health promotion strategy aimed at informing, influencing, and assisting individuals and organizations to take greater responsibility and become more active in matters affecting mental and physical health. The goal was to develop lifestyles that maintain and enhance well-being. By the mid-1980s, at least two publications contributed to a broader definition of health promotion that emphasized empowerment and environmental factors. In 1984, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Europe defined health promotion as the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health. In addition to lifestyle changes, the WHO Regional Office advocated for methods such as legislation, fiscal measures, organizational change, community development, and spontaneous local activities to combat health hazards. In 1986, Jake Epp, the Canadian Minister of National Health and Welfare, released Achieving Health for All: A Framework for Health Promotion, also known as the Epp Report. This report identified three mechanisms of health promotion: self-care, mutual aid (actions people take to help each other cope), and healthy environments. The WHO, in collaboration with other organizations, has co-sponsored several international conferences on health promotion, including: The 1st International Conference on Health Promotion in Ottawa in 1986, which resulted in the Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion. This charter emphasized advocacy for health, equity in health, and coordinated action by governments, health and social sectors, non-governmental organizations, local authorities, industry, and the media. It also stressed the need to adapt health promotion strategies to the local needs and contexts of individual countries and regions. The 2nd International Conference on Health Promotion in Adelaide in 1988, which produced the Adelaide Recommendations on Healthy Public Policy. The 3rd International Conference on Health Promotion in Sundsvall in 1991, which led to the Sundsvall Statement on Supportive Environments for Health. The 4th International Conference on Health Promotion in Jakarta in 1997, which resulted in the Jakarta Declaration on Leading Health Promotion into the 21st Century. The 5th Global Conference on Health Promotion in Mexico City in 2000, which produced the Mexico Ministerial Statement for the Promotion of Health. The 6th Global Conference on Health Promotion in Bangkok in 2005, which resulted in the Bangkok Charter for Health Promotion in a Globalized World. Collectively, the documents produced by these conferences emphasized the importance of investing in health promotion beyond an individual, disease-oriented, behavior-change model. Health promotion can be implemented in various settings, including communities, healthcare facilities, schools, and workplaces. Worksite health promotion, also referred to as workplace health promotion, is defined as the combined efforts of employers, employees, and society to improve the health and well-being of people at work. The WHO has identified the workplace as a priority setting for health promotion in the 21st century because it influences physical, mental, economic, and social well-being and provides an ideal infrastructure to support health promotion for a large audience. Worksite health promotion programs, also known as workplace wellness programs, often include initiatives such as exercise, nutrition, smoking cessation, and stress management. Evidence regarding the effectiveness of these programs varies. For example, some studies have shown positive effects on dietary intake, while evidence for physical activity and health risk indicators remains inconclusive. A meta-analysis of 46 studies published between 1970 and 2005 found moderate, statistically significant effects of workplace health promotion, particularly exercise, on work ability and overall well-being. Additionally, activities promoting healthy lifestyles appeared to reduce sickness absences. Another meta-analysis of 22 studies published between 1997 and 2007 found that workplace health promotion interventions led to small reductions in depression and anxiety. Globally, government agencies and non-governmental organizations have made substantial efforts in health promotion. Examples include: International and Multinational Efforts: The WHO and its regional offices, such as the Pan American Health Organization, play a significant role in global health promotion. The International Union for Health Promotion and Education, based in France, organizes international, regional, and national conferences. Australia: The Australian Health Promotion Association, established in 1988, is a professional body dedicated to health promotion. In 2008, the National Health and Hospitals Reform Commission recommended the establishment of a national health promotion agency. ACT Health in the Australian Capital Territory supports health promotion through funding and information dissemination. The Victorian Health Promotion Foundation (VicHealth) in the state of Victoria was the world's first health promotion foundation. Canada: In 2005, the province of Ontario appointed a health promotion minister to lead its Ministry of Health Promotion. The Canadian Health Network, which provided reliable online health information, was discontinued in 2007. The BC Coalition for Health Promotion is a grassroots, voluntary non-profit organization dedicated to advancing health promotion in British Columbia. New Zealand: The Health Promotion Forum of New Zealand serves as the national umbrella organization for over 150 organizations committed to improving health. United Kingdom: CHAPS is a partnership of community-based organizations coordinated by the Terrence Higgins Trust, focusing on HIV health promotion for gay men in England and Wales. In 2008, the Royal Society for the Promotion of Health merged with the Royal Institute of Public Health to form the Royal Society for Public Health. The Health Promotion Agency for Northern Ireland provides leadership and strategic direction for health promotion in the region. United States: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has a Coordinating Center for Health Promotion, whose mission is to prevent disease, improve health, and enhance human potential through evidence-based interventions and research. The U.S. Army Center for Health Promotion and Preventive Medicine provides worldwide technical support for implementing preventive medicine, public health, and wellness services within the Army. Other entities include the Public Health Education and Health Promotion Section of the American Public Health Association, the Wellness Council of America, and URAC, which accredits comprehensive wellness programs focusing on health promotion, chronic disease prevention, and health risk reduction.
